title: Ok, this is nuts. After three months i finally reached a point where i can DIRECT an animation
author: milox88
selftext:
I'm developing *L'Eredità Bellini*, a hand-drawn-style 2D point-and-click adventure inspired by classics like Broken Sword. For the past three months, character animation has been an absolute nightmare. I experimented with Blender, Mixamo, custom animation pipelines, AI video generation, and pretty much every workaround I could think of.

My goal sounded simple: take rigged 3D characters, animate them, and render consistent 2D sprites that actually fit the game's art style. But I wanted something more than just playing predefined animations. I wanted to **DIRECT my characters**, without spending hours manually adjusting bones and keyframes.

Yesterday, I gave Claude the task of building a completely new animation tool.

A few hours later, I had a working **BELLINI ANIMATION FARM**. And I genuinely can't believe what it does.

Here's what I've got working so far:

* **Natural-language animation direction:** I type something like "stand composed, clasp your hands, then bow" (in Italian!), and the character performs the action.
* **Character personalities:** I describe a character's personality, and the system adjusts posture, walking style, gestures, energy, and body language accordingly.
* **Personality-based animation suggestions:** It proposes animations that fit each character's behavior.
* **Script-aware animation suggestions:** It reads my actual game's dialogue files and suggests gestures and reactions based on what characters are saying.
* **Manual adjustments:** I can fine-tune poses, movements, timing, and body language through visual controls.
* **Seated characters:** It supports sitting, talking, and interacting with tables using actual character and furniture dimensions.
* **8-direction sprite rendering:** It automatically renders animations into 2D sprite atlases compatible with my Godot project.
* **Fast rendering:** On my humble RTX 2060 12GB, a 96-frame, 8-direction walking animation takes roughly 14 seconds to render.

The best part?

**The animation engine itself doesn't require AI inference or API calls.**

It uses Godot, Mixamo animations, procedural rules, IK, and reusable animation recipes. Claude helps extend the system when I need a gesture it doesn't know how to perform. It's not perfect yet. Some gestures need adjustments, facial animation is still missing, and I still need to finish integrating the exported animations into the actual game's runtime.

But the core pipeline WORKS.

After three months of fighting animation tools, I can finally type what I want a character to do, adjust the performance, and export the result. I'm no longer just trying to make sprites move.

**I'm actually directing my characters.**

And that's a pretty incredible feeling for a solo indie developer.

I'll share some footage once I've polished a few remaining issues.

Just wanted to share this little victory. It's been a hell of a journey.

comments.author: TopIntelligent8802
comments.body: i don't really understand how this program works from your explanation. Can you elaborate on the how claude actually creates the animation?

replies.author: milox88
replies.body:
Sure! I probably didn't explain that part clearly enough.

Claude doesn't generate the animation frames directly. Claude actually wrote the animation software itself.

Here's how it works:

1. 3D character: I import a rigged FBX character (Mixamo-compatible) into my custom Godot-based Animation Farm.

2. Base animations: The program uses existing Mixamo animation clips as a starting point. It can also combine them with procedural movements and custom gesture recipes.

3. Natural-language direction: I can type something like "stand composed, clasp your hands, then bow." A rule-based parser translates that instruction into an animation recipe, which the program executes using skeletal transformations, blending and IK.

4. Character personality: I describe the character (for example, "a cheerful, curious 30-year-old" or "a tired 60-year-old manual worker"). The program extracts personality parameters and uses them to modify posture, stride, arm movement and other aspects of the animation.

5. Rendering: Godot renders the animated 3D character into 2D frames from eight different camera directions, then packages everything into sprite atlases for my point-and-click game.

So where does Claude come in?

Claude developed the application, its animation logic, procedural systems, personality handling and export pipeline.

When I need a completely new gesture that the software doesn't support yet, Claude can also help create a new animation recipe in JSON, which I can import into the Farm.

The important distinction is that Claude isn't generating a new AI video every time I request an animation. The actual animation and rendering happen locally, using deterministic procedural techniques.

That's also why it's so fast: I can render a 96-frame, eight-direction walking animation in about 14 seconds on an RTX 2060 12GB.

It's essentially a custom animation director built with Claude's help, rather than a text-to-video generator.

Hope that makes more sense!

comments.author: milox88
comments.body:
Here's the first actual footage of the Animation Farm!

Same character, same base walking animation, three different personality configurations:

- No personality: Default walk.
- Curious, cheerful, 30 years old: A more energetic walking style.
- 60 years old, physically demanding job: A more tired, hunched posture with a different stride.

The interesting part is that these aren't three manually animated walking cycles.

The Farm procedurally modifies the character's movement based on personality traits, using the same underlying animation.

Everything runs locally in Godot, with no generative video inference required.

Still plenty of room for improvement, especially in making subtle personality differences more visible, but I'm pretty excited about where this is going! [animation farm test](https://youtube.com/shorts/2jlOj6GrGXk?is=rnMDlW1mi74U5ozE)

replies.author: milox88
replies.body:
I'm not looking for pats on the back or compliments.

I just wanted to show how a problem that kept me up at night for months could eventually be solved with a relatively simple, purpose-built tool.

For me, Animation Farm represents a major milestone in my development workflow. And the irony is that, despite being built with the help of AI, it actually reduces my dependence on AI for the animation process.

That's what I wanted to share. Not how impressive the tool is, but how much of a difference the right tool can make.
